title: Authoring Tools for Designing Intelligent Tutoring Systems: a Systematic Review of the Literature
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
extended_summary: This paper addresses the question of how authoring tools have been supporting the design of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) for non-programmer authors. The authors note that, although ITS are effective and widely studied, building them remains costly and authoring tools may reduce the technical burden. To synthesize the state of the evidence, they conducted a systematic literature review covering studies published from January 2009 to June 2016.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review with explicit search, selection, and quality-assessment procedures, but it is not a primary causal study or meta-analysis. The evidence is synthesized from heterogeneous studies, many of which are illustrative or non-empirical, so credibility is moderate rather than high for outcome claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive design-process benefits for ITS authoring tools, but it does not report pooled quantitative effects on learner outcomes or operational gains with an effect size threshold. The impact is therefore suggestive and useful for the field, but modest/unclear in K-12 evidence terms.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of authoring tools used to design classical ITSs for non-programmer authors, including model-tracing/cognitive tutors, example-tracing tutors, constraint-based tutors, dialog-based tutors, and other ITS variants.

finding.finding_summary: The review found empirical evidence that ITS authoring tools improve the efficiency of ITS design, mainly by reducing authoring effort and supporting faster production for non-programmer authors. Across the 33 included studies, the reported benefits also included improved quality of authored artifacts and usability, but the paper does not provide a pooled effect size; the evidence is summarized qualitatively from the primary studies.
finding.measure: Authoring efficiency / development effort, usability, and quality of authored artifacts reported in included studies
finding.study_size: n=33 studies (systematic review of 33 primary studies; 15 empirically evaluated)

finding.finding_summary: The paper concludes that ITS authoring tools may broaden access to ITS creation by enabling non-programmer authors, increasing the number and diversity of available tutors and extending participation in tutor development. This is a synthesis-level claim about potential institutional impact rather than a measured student outcome, and no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Breadth of tutor development participation, availability/diversity of authored tutors
